165.t: His father faces down a Kentucky sheriff
165.s: His father pulls up a sheriff in Kentucky; later the funeral and the white preacher on the porch.
165.q: Oh yeah. Oh he was something. I saw him stand up to a sheriff down south with a gun on his hip during the days when there were people being lynched every day. And he physically pulled the sheriff up out of his chair.

165.t: Learning not to be angry at slurs, and advice to his son Eric
165.s: After mobsters rubbed his head for luck, he reasoned anger accepts the insult, and later taught his son in England the same lesson.
165.q: That’s not me. What are you getting mad at? Because if you’re mad, then you’re a nigger. I said, no, that ain’t me. So then I learned, I’m not going to get mad. I applied that lesson to my son many years later, when he was in school in England. I took my four kids to London. We’ll get to that…

508.t: Reading Twain aloud for Mrs. Dewey and his father's Emmett Till lesson
508.s: His fourth-grade teacher made him read the n-word aloud, and his father used Emmett Till to teach him not to let others define him.
508.q: Fourth grade, fifth grade, sixth grade, seventh grade. I mean you know, it was like this thing. Mrs. Dewey, my fourth grade teacher, she loved reading Mark Twain, but she didn’t like black people, so she would always have me read the pages with the word “nigger” on it in a class full of white…

508.t: Father's lesson on grandparents and Jim Crow: nobody gets to define you
508.s: His father compares the cage seating on buses his grandparents endured, leading Branford to declare at nineteen that others do not define him.
508.q: My paternal grandparents and my maternal grandmother. He said, “Your grandparents had to go through a lot worse shit than that. You’ll never know. It’s like your grandfather, if he said the wrong thing, it could get him killed. You’ll never know nothing about that.” He said, “Them buses you ride on…

917.t: Father's Creole appearance during the riot
917.s: Father, light-skinned Creole, could pass in the streets unmolested; reflections on telling who is who.
917.q: No, my father wasn't mixed up in it. Because my father, he could pass around the streets. And they wouldn't worry him. Because my father was a Creole. And you know, in Creole, well, my father was kind of bright.

254.t: White and Black neighbors in St. John Parish
254.s: She describes mixed communities in her country childhood and her father's relationship with a white man.
254.q: That was the richest white man out there. And he has the biggest white people. Where he sat down. That was the best. And empty. When they build a big school for the white folks. Him and my father have to top seat together. He couldn't speak French and my father couldn't speak English. They both…

577.t: Racial makeup of the neighborhood and his insurance collecting route
577.s: The area was mostly white with some Black residents and is all Black now; he describes his insurance debit route there.
577.q: There's always been colored back there. Yeah. But it was mostly white, there was a lot of white people back there. Yeah. You know, you take all over towards, a little bit further over to Monroe Street there, there was always a few colors.

836.t: Church at Ascension near Donaldsonville; no segregation then
836.s: Buggy rides to Mass, her christening and communion at the old church, and the lack of segregation in those days.
836.q: We, uh, well right out to Thibodeau. We'd go, my mother would drive us when I was a little girl, about 10 years old. We used to go to Thibodeau to Mass. And that's about 10 miles or something. Well, she'd have this horse on her. Well, it wasn't a, it wasn't a surrey. It was a buggy. Do you know…

311.t: The union merger and integrated schools
311.s: The merged unions brought camaraderie; he describes integrated schools, Polytechnic High and his poor family.
311.q: Yes. Well that was very good because then we could really go to the same meetings and we had camaraderie together and things like that, and so that was a lot of help. That’s the way it should be, because that’s how I grew up. I grew up — see I’m not one of these guys that just came from the south…

360.t: Segregation, schools and movies in a mixed neighborhood
360.s: Subtle segregation in schools and theaters while growing up among Polish, Lithuanian and Slavic neighbors; Buck Jones and Tom Mix movies.
360.q: There were, but it was just an accepted thing. That didn’t bother us. As a matter of fact, the neighborhood that I grew up in was predominantly Polish, Lithuanian, and Slavish. There were only three colored families at that time. That’s what we were, we were colored at that time. Only three colored…

417.t: Playing for white classmates at an integrated high school
417.s: Back at Conley Vocational High, he learns instrumentals for white students and finds that fights end in handshakes.
417.q: Great. I’m finished with the Letche Elementary School. I’m in high school. That’s when I got in all the trouble with the gangs and so forth. I’m 15. I miss a semester. But remember, I was always a year ahead of everybody anyway. I miss a semester in school. I came back. Started going to school. The…

224.t: The mixed neighborhood and integrated schools
224.s: He describes the French-Canadian, Jewish, Irish and Southern black neighbors and how schools on the hill differed in makeup.
224.q: Yeah. You say describe the neighborhood. Okay. On the right-hand side of us there were French-Canadian people. There was a man there that looked like Fred Astaire. He would have his derby on, and the whole thing. He wouldn’t say much. His moustache and his umbrella all the time. He would look like…

226.t: White teachers and why small minorities meet little segregation
226.s: His white teachers treated him fine, and he reasons that segregation problems arise only when a minority becomes large.
226.q: Okay, fine. I don’t have any problems with them. See, any time you have a society – I’ve learned that much in life – any time you have a society where the minority is not that great – in other words, it doesn’t cause too much of a – make too many waves or cause too much of a problem – you don’t…

373.s: Almost no black students then; he notes later desegregation and the separate Girls Latin School.
373.q: No, there were very few blacks then. That took a lot of doing. That happened when finally the Supreme Court said that in public schools, segregated education was inherently unconstitutional. Then Boston became a storm center there. But eventually, when I come back there now, there are a lot of…

1.t: First manicure and the word delicatessen
1.s: The two boys were chased from a barber-shop window after watching a manicure and marveled at the word delicatessen.
1.ch: Chicago, Lee Collins and the road
1.q: The first time I'd seen a manicure. I seen this cat sittin' in a barber chair, me and my uncle. He was getting a shave and getting a haircut, and had this woman playing with his hands. So me and my uncle, we ...(?)... [LAUGHS] We were lookin' in the window...! And the woman looked at us, the barber…

65.s: Haitians came to cut cane and return home; Machito says minor trades were left to blacks and compares to Jewish holidays in New York.
65.q: Well, the Haitians they had no way out since they are black, so they went out there with the purpose just to cut the cane and come back to Haiti.

9.t: A mixed neighborhood and integrated schools
9.s: The Warwick Street house had White and Black families; the school was integrated, and Black teachers arrived before he finished grammar school.
9.ch: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
9.q: Mixed. Because the house I lived in on Warwick Street, we were on the ground floor, our family, and right above us was a White family, and above them was another Black family.

90.s: Unloading for store owners then being pelted with fruit, and gangs harassing children delivering white families' laundry.
90.q: But the people, they just... It's a strange, strange love goes on in that South, you know. A strange love. For instance, like, at the big chain stores that I was talking about earlier...I was talking about Piggly-Wiggly, A&P and those stores... Now, you would go and help those guys

382.t: Black population of Homestead and the steel mills
382.s: The Black community grew with migration from the South to work in the mills; ethnic mix of Hungarians and Poles; school segregation.
382.ch: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
382.q: Well, let's see -- there were quite a few families -- in fact Chet Campbell's family was one of the original families to live in Homestead. I would say there might have been about ten or fifteen black families that would be the first families to live there.

386.t: Surviving as a black child in Texas
386.s: He talks about danger from police, the reform school at Gatesville and humility demanded of blacks.
386.q: Well, as a child, it was not more difficult for me than for it was/my parents. My parents were the ones that had...my father...he was the mayor, the black mayor. He was in the most danger. Because if a black kid did something in Texas, they'd just send him away to a reform school and they'd keep…

31.t: Being one of few black children in Everett schools
31.s: He tells of fighting classmates who used racial insults, and he and Hinton note black children got the same schooling as whites.
31.q: No, it was only about three colored families around there, see. Let me see, in my class in grammar school there was only two colored, Rufus Snowden and I.

125.t: School athletics and first interest in golf in Colorado Springs
125.s: In an integrated Colorado Springs school he ran track, played basketball, had a run-in with a biased teacher, and took up golf.
125.q: interested in sports, more or less, I guess through that facility. And naturally in the gym of the public schools, as I said. As early as this time we were living then in Colorado Springs, Colorado, and this was an integrated school. Now, I can remember some incidents of that integrated school…

79.t: Lincoln's history as a segregated school in a prejudiced town
79.s: Lincoln was founded by Civil War veterans, had 300 students, was coed and accredited. Jefferson City was as prejudiced as Webster Groves.
79.q: ... AND A very prejudiced town. I mean it's not more prejudiced than Webster Groves because you had the same situation that happened and dastardly. Total resentment about them, you know.
